Confusing electoral theater (WHAT parties promise) with genuine systemic safety (WHO actually benefits). The focus is partisan survival.

Parties run a Smart Selfish Maneuver, manufacturing tough-on-crime pretexts to capture anxious voters while avoiding costly upstream solutions.

Promising justice and safety while delivering punitive spectacle leads straight to systemic failure.

The Unavoidable Truth: Electoral competition forces parties into superficial, punitive policy auctions.

The Unavoidable Lie: Stated tough-on-crime measures are framed as genuine community protection.

Parties trade long-term structural prevention for short-term electoral theater, weaponizing tragedy for votes.

The major parties are pitching their policies to voters just two days before early voting opens in the Victorian election.

The Liberals have announced proposed new anti-stalking laws, dubbed Celeste's Law after murder victim Celeste Manno.

Labor leader Ben Carroll is pledging to slash public hospital waiting lists with a $1.2 billion investment.

By Tim Callanan

The Greens have taken a pop at both Labor and the Liberals over their policies on addressing youth crime.

The Liberals announced a $60 million policy which would enable judges to sentence some youth offenders to a stint in boot camp.

Labor last week unveiled a plan to sentence mid-level youth offenders to detention for up to 12 months.

Greens justice spokesperson Katherine Copsey isn't impressed with either approach.

"Labor and the Liberals are locked in a grotesque competition to see who can announce the cruellest headline and lock up the most children," she says.

"Jess Wilson wants to send kids to prison boot camps to do farm labour. Ben Carroll wants to lock them up for a year and call it therapy.

"Neither has a serious plan to stop children entering the justice system in the first place."

The Greens say they would invest in early intervention, youth diversion and expanded mental health services to address youth crime.

By Tim Callanan

With just 12 days to go before the election, Labor's primary vote shows little sign of turning around.

Pollster Kos Samaras from Redbridge Group says his organisation's polling now paints a poor picture for Labor in terms of primary vote.

"Very clear that the Labor Party's trailing in the polls. They're now around the low 20s. They were polling in the mid-20s for a good part of this year," he tells 774 ABC Melbourne.

Samaras, who is a former Labor strategist, says it's a better story for the Liberals, whose primary vote is slowly climbing.

"The difference with them is that they have gone from the mid-20s to about the low 30s now, and this is why they are well positioned to win this election."

Samaras says both parties left their campaign launches late and it will be tough to make an impact on voters this late in the game.
